claims.text: Adding approximately 2 at.% B by substitution on a transition-metal site in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 will improve glass-forming ability.
The approximately 2 at.% B addition will increase the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
B addition will produce strong P-B chemical bonds in the amorphous alloy.
P-B bonds will reinforce and increase the connectivity of the amorphous network.
The proposed P-B-bonded network will restrict local atomic mobility.
B has a small atomic size and a propensity for covalent bonding with phosphorus.
Reduced atomic mobility caused by B will increase the activation energy for crystallization.
The B-doped alloy will have a higher DSC crystallization-onset temperature than the undoped baseline.
The B-doped alloy will show less crystallinity than the baseline under identical rapid-cooling conditions.
Arc melting followed by melt-spinning at approximately 10^5 K/s yields an amorphous Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy.
The amorphous structure of melt-spun Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 was confirmed by XRD and TEM.
DSC confirmed that the baseline alloy was amorphous.
Very rapid cooling is required for the cited Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy to become amorphous, whereas slower cooling produces crystalline phases.
Phosphorus and high mixing entropy promote glass formation in rapidly cooled Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
B segregation and boride formation may negate the proposed beneficial effect.
Uniform B distribution is critical to obtaining the proposed improvement.
A failure to obtain a statistically significant increase in crystallization-onset temperature would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that the intervention is not expected to work when B segregates or borides form, but the falsification rule treats observation of that excluded condition as falsifying the hypothesis. A valid decisive test should assess the predicted benefit after uniform B incorporation without boride formation.
